name: Visual Scene Statistics — Prediction Error Reduction via Efficient Coding

mechanism_chain.description: Visual stimulus with 1/f spatial frequency amplitude spectrum (power law exponent β ≈ 2.0–2.4) → sparse activation of orientation-selective V1 simple cells. Olshausen & Field (1996): V1 receptive fields are optimally matched to natural image statistics via sparse coding — fewer active neurons required, lower metabolic expenditure per unit information conveyed.

data.finding: V1 receptive fields emerge from sparse coding optimization for natural image statistics; ~6,000 citations confirm that V1 neurons are matched to 1/f power spectrum of natural scenes
data.paradigm: Computational sparse coding model trained on natural images
data.effect: ICA/sparse coding recovers Gabor-like V1 receptive fields
data.design: Computational model with natural image patches

data.finding: V1 neurons respond more sparsely (fewer neurons activated) to natural vs. phase-scrambled stimuli, confirming efficient coding prediction
data.paradigm: Electrophysiology in macaque V1 during natural scene viewing
data.effect: Lifetime sparseness increased from 0.4 to 0.8 for natural vs. scrambled

data.finding: Fractal dimension D ≈ 1.3 produces 60% lower GSR and peak aesthetic preference across multiple paradigms
data.source: Taylor et al. (2005); Hagerhall et al. (2008)
data.paradigm: Psychophysiology (GSR) + preference rating during fractal pattern viewing
data.effect: 60% GSR reduction at D ≈ 1.3 vs. non-fractal; preference peak at D = 1.1–1.5

justification.backing: The warrant connecting 1/f spectral statistics to V1 efficient coding rests on Olshausen & Field's foundational result (ICA on natural images recovers V1-like receptive fields) and Vinje & Gallant's neural confirmation (sparse coding in vivo for natural stimuli). Taylor's fractal work and Coburn's architectural beauty data (β = 0.31, R² ≈ 0.10 for fractal dimension) provide the architectural translation evidence. The convergence across computational modeling, single-unit physiology, psychophysics, and architectural preference studies increases credence substantially.
justification.qualifier: MECHANISM warrant at 0.65 reflects strong V1-level evidence but acknowledges that the architectural application extends sparse coding beyond its training domain (natural images). Olshausen (panel debate) contested the transfer to rectilinear architecture: buildings with modular grids have power concentrated at specific spatial frequencies, not distributed as power law. The confidence applies most strongly to organic/fractal architecture (D = 1.1–1.5) and less strongly to minimalist rectilinear facades where 1/f statistics are absent.
justification.rebuttal: The claim would fail if: (a) V1 efficient coding for natural image statistics does not extend to architectural stimuli — Olshausen argued that rectilinear architecture falls outside V1's natural-statistics operating range, which would invalidate the transfer for modernist facades; (b) the fractal dimension-preference relationship is an artifact of familiarity rather than efficient coding — more natural-looking patterns may simply be more familiar, and the mechanism would be prototype matching (Carbon & Leder) rather than coding efficiency; (c) Taylor's D = 1.3 optimum is stimulus-specific and does not generalize to complex multi-scale architectural scenes where local D varies across the facade.

competing_accounts.account: Familiarity/prototype matching rather than efficient coding
competing_accounts.claim: Aesthetic preference for fractal patterns reflects familiarity with natural scenes (prototype matching) rather than coding efficiency per se
competing_accounts.implication_for_template: If prototype matching, the mechanism is evaluative (later, ~300ms+) rather than perceptual (early V1, ~50-100ms). T1 confidence would decrease by ~0.10 and the warrant might shift toward EMPIRICAL_COVARIANCE since the mechanism would be cognitive rather than perceptual.

competing_accounts.account: Architectural stimuli outside natural-statistics operating range
competing_accounts.claim: Rectilinear architecture has non-1/f spectral properties (power at grid frequencies) and therefore does not engage V1 efficient coding in the same way as natural scenes
competing_accounts.implication_for_template: If correct, T1 applies only to organic/biomorphic architecture, not to the majority of modern buildings. The template would need an architectural_type moderator splitting the confidence: 0.65 for organic, 0.40 for rectilinear.

mechanism_chain.description: Sparse V1 codes generate feedback predictions via the predictive coding hierarchy (Rao & Ballard, 1999). When V1 efficiently codes the stimulus, the mismatch between feedforward input and feedback prediction is small — low prediction error. Estimated 40–60% reduction in prediction error magnitude for natural vs. phase-scrambled scenes (Muckli et al., 2015).

data.finding: V1 activity in occluded regions reflects top-down predictions; feedback signals carry predictions about expected visual content
data.paradigm: fMRI of V1 during visual occlusion paradigm
data.effect: V1 BOLD in occluded regions encodes scene-context predictions (decodable with MVPA)

data.finding: Predicted visual stimuli reduce BOLD signal in V1 relative to unpredicted stimuli
data.effect: Expected gratings → reduced V1 BOLD vs. unexpected (within-subjects)

data.finding: Hierarchical predictive coding model accounts for V1 response properties including end-stopping and extraclassical receptive field effects
data.effect: Model predicts V1 response suppression for predictable stimuli and enhancement for unpredictable stimuli
data.design: Computational model validated against V1 physiology

justification.backing: The warrant connecting efficient coding to reduced PE rests on the predictive processing framework implementation in visual cortex. Muckli's occlusion studies demonstrate that V1 feedback carries predictions, and Kok et al. show that prediction confirmation suppresses V1 activity. The 40-60% PE reduction estimate for natural vs. scrambled scenes is derived from comparing BOLD responses to predicted vs. unpredicted stimuli in the Kok et al. and Summerfield et al. paradigms.
justification.qualifier: Confidence 0.65 reflects strong mechanistic evidence at the V1 level. The 40-60% PE reduction range is estimated from BOLD signal changes, which are an indirect measure of neural prediction error. The relationship between BOLD suppression and actual PE magnitude is assumed to be approximately linear, which may not hold at extreme values. The estimate applies to passive viewing of static images; active exploration with saccadic scanning will modulate PE through additional mechanisms.
justification.rebuttal: The claim would fail if: (a) BOLD suppression for predicted stimuli reflects sharpened representations (fewer neurons firing at higher rates) rather than overall PE reduction — de Lange et al. (2018) argue that sharpening, not silencing, is the primary effect, which would preserve coding efficiency but not necessarily reduce total PE magnitude; (b) feedback signals to V1 carry task-relevant bias rather than predictions per se, making the PE interpretation contingent on task demands rather than stimulus statistics alone.

competing_accounts.claim: Predicted stimuli produce sparser, more precise V1 representations rather than reduced overall activity — coding efficiency improves but total neural energy may not decrease
competing_accounts.implication_for_template: If sharpening dominates, Step 3 (metabolic savings) would be weakened but Step 2 (PE reduction in terms of information theory) would be preserved. Net effect on T1 confidence approximately neutral, but the mechanism pathway description would need qualification.

mechanism_chain.description: Lower prediction error magnitude → smaller mismatch signals requiring upward propagation → reduced synaptic transmission load. Laughlin & Sejnowski (2003): cortical metabolic cost is proportional to synaptic transmission. Estimated 10–20% glucose utilization reduction in early visual cortex.

data.finding: Cortical metabolic cost scales with synaptic transmission volume; synaptic transmission consumes approximately 75% of cortical energy budget
data.paradigm: Biophysical modeling of neural energy budgets
data.effect: 75% of cortical energy allocated to synaptic signaling

data.finding: Predicted visual stimuli reduce BOLD signal in V1 relative to unpredicted stimuli
data.effect: Expected gratings → reduced V1 BOLD vs. unexpected (within-subjects)

data.finding: Repetition of expected stimuli produces greater suppression than repetition of unexpected stimuli in V1
data.effect: Interaction: expectation × repetition in V1 BOLD

justification.backing: The warrant connecting PE reduction to metabolic savings rests on two independent lines of evidence: (a) biophysical energy budgets establishing that synaptic transmission dominates cortical energy expenditure (Laughlin & Sejnowski, 2003; Attwell & Laughlin, 2001), and (b) neuroimaging evidence that predictable stimuli reduce cortical activation in early visual areas (Kok et al., 2012; Summerfield et al., 2008). The convergence across biophysical modeling and fMRI paradigms increases credence beyond what either line alone would support. The inference assumes that BOLD signal reduction reflects reduced neural metabolic demand rather than a redistribution of processing.
justification.qualifier: The 10-20% glucose reduction estimate is extrapolated from single-neuron biophysics to population-level cortical processing. This extrapolation assumes approximately linear scaling from individual synapses to cortical columns, which may not hold if network-level dynamics introduce nonlinearities. The estimate applies to early visual cortex during passive viewing. Active visual exploration, sustained attention, and task demands will modulate the effect. No study has directly measured glucose utilization in human visual cortex as a function of stimulus statistical predictability. Confidence 0.50 with THEORETICAL_DEFAULT flag reflects the gap between mechanism-level evidence and the specific architectural claim.
justification.rebuttal: The claim would fail if: (a) predictive coding correction signals are metabolically cheap relative to feedforward processing, making PE reduction negligible for total cortical energy — Lennie (2003) argues that the energy cost of neural signaling is small relative to maintenance costs, which would make PE-driven metabolic savings functionally trivial; (b) reduced PE in early visual cortex is compensated by increased processing in higher-order areas generating the predictions, producing no net metabolic savings at the whole-brain level; (c) the BOLD signal reduction for predicted stimuli reflects sharpened representations rather than overall reduced activity — the sharpening account would preserve information-theoretic efficiency without metabolic savings.

competing_accounts.proponent: Kok et al. (2012); de Lange, Heilbron, & Kok (2018)
competing_accounts.claim: Prediction reduces BOLD not because total energy expenditure decreases but because neural representations become sparser and more precise — fewer neurons fire but carry more information per spike
competing_accounts.implication_for_template: If sharpening rather than silencing, the metabolic savings may be smaller than estimated (possibly negligible), but the coding efficiency gain and downstream PE reduction still hold. T1's aesthetic prediction (efficient coding → positive valence) is preserved under both accounts; the metabolic pathway (step 3) would be weakened but the information-theoretic pathway would be strengthened. Net effect on template confidence: approximately neutral, but the mechanism description should acknowledge both pathways.

mechanism_chain.description: Reduced processing cost → positive valence signal (Joffily & Coricelli, 2013). Coburn et al. (2020): fractal dimension β = 0.31 predicting architectural beauty ratings (R² contribution ≈ 0.10). Taylor et al. (2005): 60% lower GSR for D ≈ 1.3 fractal patterns. Architectural facades with D = 1.1–1.5 preferred over non-fractal facades.

data.finding: Fractal dimension predicts architectural beauty ratings with β = 0.31 (R² ≈ 0.10 for D alone; R² ≈ 0.35 with edge density + curvature entropy)
data.paradigm: Image-computable metrics predicting beauty ratings of architectural photographs
data.effect: β = 0.31 for fractal dimension; R² = 0.35 for combined visual statistics

data.finding: Free-energy reduction produces positive valence signal via interoceptive prediction confirmation
data.paradigm: Computational model linking free-energy dynamics to emotional valence
data.effect: Decreasing free energy → positive valence; increasing → negative valence

data.finding: Viewing fractal patterns at D ≈ 1.3 produces 60% GSR reduction compared to non-fractal controls
data.paradigm: GSR measurement during fractal pattern viewing
data.design: Within-subjects comparison of fractal vs. non-fractal stimuli

justification.backing: The bridge from reduced metabolic demand to positive aesthetic response rests on two convergent lines: (a) Joffily & Coricelli's computational free-energy account linking PE reduction to positive valence, which provides the theoretical bridge; and (b) Coburn et al.'s large-scale empirical study demonstrating that visual statistics predicting coding efficiency (fractal dimension) predict architectural beauty ratings. The physiological confirmation from Hagerhall's GSR data provides a third independent line. Coburn's R² = 0.35 ceiling for combined visual statistics sets an important bound on explanatory power: no single visual feature template should claim more than ~35% of aesthetic variance.
justification.qualifier: EMPIRICAL_COVARIANCE at 0.55 reflects the strongest step in the architectural translation chain but acknowledges that (a) R² = 0.10 for fractal dimension alone means ~90% of beauty variance is explained by other factors; (b) the Joffily & Coricelli free-energy-to-valence model is computational, not directly tested neurally; (c) architectural beauty ratings are collected from photographs, not immersive environments (Coburn panel comment: −10% adjustment for immersive experience). Confidence should not exceed 0.65 for any single-feature architectural prediction.
justification.rebuttal: The claim would fail if: (a) the free-energy-to-positive-valence link is incorrect — alternative accounts (appraisal theory, prototype matching) explain aesthetic preference without invoking metabolic efficiency; (b) Coburn's R² = 0.10 for fractal dimension alone is too small to be architecturally meaningful — the effect may be statistically significant in large samples but practically negligible for design decisions; (c) GSR reduction for fractals reflects relaxation/habituation rather than positive aesthetic response — the stress reduction and the beauty judgment may have different mechanisms.

competing_accounts.claim: Aesthetic pleasure arises from processing fluency (ease of stimulus processing) rather than metabolic efficiency per se — the mechanism is meta-cognitive (monitoring processing ease) rather than metabolic
competing_accounts.implication_for_template: If fluency rather than metabolic efficiency, the mechanism pathway changes but the prediction remains similar: 1/f stimuli are more fluently processed → positive affect. The confidence level would be similar, but the warrant description would shift from biophysical to cognitive. Step 3 (metabolic) would be less relevant; a direct Step 2→4 pathway via processing fluency would be more parsimonious.

visual_complexity.source: Taylor et al. (2005); Hagerhall et al. (2004); Coburn et al. (2020)
visual_complexity.notes: D < 1.1: visually impoverished. D = 1.1–1.5: aesthetic range. D ≈ 1.3 optimal; peak GSR reduction ~60% vs. non-fractal. D > 1.5: increasing complexity approaching visual noise.

interaction_templates.nature: T1 is the luminance-and-texture channel of T2's general complexity Goldilocks. T1 specifies WHICH complexity dimension (spatial frequency statistics) engages efficient coding.

T1 measures APERIODIC multi-scale structure (fractal); VF2 measures PERIODIC rhythmic regularity. Partial independence confirmed by Coburn (ΔR² after controlling T1: VF2 SCI ≈ 0.03). Compute jointly to avoid double-counting.
Dappled light has 1/f luminance statistics — T1 and L1 converge at this configuration. Joint activation is additive.
T1 is Channel 1 (fractal fluency) of VIEW1's five-channel model.

panel_reasoning_excerpt:
### Step 4: Prediction Generation via Interventionist Reasoning
*(Woodward, 2003; incorporating R6, R7, R8)*

**Input**: Completed mechanism trace(s) from Step 3.
**Operation**: Apply prediction generation grammar — formal operations that interrogate each intervention point in the trace.
**Output**: A set of predictions, each tagged with derivation chain, confidence, prediction level, and cause type.

**Revised Prediction Generation Grammar** (10 operations, expanded from 8):

| # | Operation | Input | Output | Basis |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | SUBSTITUTE_CAUSE | Trace + alternative cause with same structural properties | Prediction: alternative cause → same effect | Woodward interventionism |
| 2 | VARY_MODERATOR | Trace + identified moderator variable | Prediction: moderator variation → effect variation | Moderation logic |
| 3 | BLOCK_PATHWAY | Trace + identified mediator | Prediction: blocking mediator → reduced/eliminated effect | Woodward interventionism |
| 4 | VARY_TEMPORAL_CONTEXT | Trace + temporal dynamics | Prediction: temporal manipulation → effect variation | Template temporal parameters |
| 5 | VARY_INDIVIDUAL | Trace + individual difference variable | Prediction: individual variation → effect variation | Individual differences |
| 6 | CROSS_CULTURAL | Trace + culturally variable parameter | Prediction: cultural variation → effect variation | Generative model calibration |
| 7 | COMBINE_MECHANISMS | Two traces with shared intermediate | Prediction: combined manipulation → combined effect (with R3 interference check) | Compositional logic |
| 8 | DOSE_RESPONSE | Trace + parameter ranges | Prediction: dose variation → response curve shape | Quantitative constraints |
| 9 | DISTINGUISH_TOTAL_VS_CONTRIBUTING | Multi-pathway trace | Prediction set: total effect vs. pathway-specific contributions (R7) | Woodward contributing cause |
| 10 | TYPE_VS_TOKEN | Any prediction | Tagged duplicate: type-level version + token-level version with required specifics (R6) | Woodward type/token |

cross_template_interactions.IC2_body_budget: T1-compliant environments reduce visual processing metabolic demand (Step 3), contributing to allostatic reserve. Chronic exposure to T1-violating environments (featureless modernism) may accumulate small but consistent allostatic costs over working hours.
